patches.reason: Clarify the common comparative patterns for one-, two-, and longer adjectives.

changes.before: TO CONSIDER 1. Adjectives can be divided into two groups: / Short (1 or 2 syllables) / Long (2 or more syllables). 2. Short adjectives take the –er + than particles: Joe is taller than Jim. 3.Long adjectives take the more + than particles: It is more expensive here than there. 4.Short adjectives that finish in –y change to I + er: She is prettier than you. 5. There are irregular adjectives: Good – Better than / Bad – Worse than. 6. We use the particles ‘as / as’ to state similarities: Joe is as tall as Jake. 7. There are adjectives who do not receive comparison degrees; those adjective have absolute meaning: This is the final test / Those people are dead. 8. Less + Adjective + than is used to state inferiority between two nouns. E.G. Alex is less determined than his brother. 9. There are three levels of comparison: Superiority , Equality and Inferiority
changes.after: TO CONSIDER 1. One-syllable adjectives usually take –er + than: Joe is taller than Jim. Some two-syllable adjectives also take –er, especially those ending in –y: pretty → prettier. Many two-syllable adjectives use more + than, and adjectives with three or more syllables normally use more + than: It is more expensive here than there. 2. There are irregular adjectives: Good → better than / bad → worse than. 3. Use as + adjective + as to state similarities: Joe is as tall as Jake. 4. Absolute adjectives do not usually take comparison degrees. 5. Less + adjective + than states inferiority. 6. There are three levels of comparison: superiority, equality, and inferiority.

The superlative for less than is: The least. E.G: That is the least of my worries. 7. ABSOLUTE adjectives do not take superlative level
changes.after: TO CONSIDER 1. One-syllable adjectives usually take –est: Joe is the tallest in his family. Some two-syllable adjectives also take –est, especially those ending in –y: pretty → prettiest. Many two-syllable adjectives use the most, and adjectives with three or more syllables normally use the most: It is the most expensive restaurant in the city. 2. Irregular forms include good → better → the best and bad → worse → the worst. 3. The superlative of less is the least. 4. Absolute adjectives do not usually take a superlative.

changes.after:
Talking about habits in the past leads us to use simple past tense structure; though, it is necessary to work with used to.

TO CONSIDER 1. Used to + base verb describes past habits or states: I used to play outside. 2. After DID, use use to in the base form: Did you use to play outside? 3. Other useful expressions: but not anymore / back in my childhood / when I was a child / when I was younger. 4. Be used to + noun or -ing describes present familiarity or a custom: She is used to reading the newspaper in the mornings.
